introduction-the-all-or-nothing-mistake.core: Teams either avoid spot entirely (and overpay) or go all-in (and risk outages). The right answer is a mix: an on-demand baseline for resilience plus spot for scalable capacity, orchestrated automatically.

first_principles.problem: A cluster runs 100% on-demand out of fear, or 100% spot and loses capacity during a reclamation wave.
truths: Spot is cheap but can be reclaimed.
Kubernetes can schedule across mixed node types.
derivation: Keep an **on-demand floor** for critical replicas.

analogy.title: Standby airline seats
analogy.story: Cheap, but you can be bumped. Book a few confirmed seats for essential travellers and fly the rest standby.
analogy.breaks: Singleton stateful workloads still belong on on-demand.

example.title: A 20/80 split
flow: Service stays up on OD + rescheduled pods

check.q: Why keep an on-demand baseline when using spot?
check.a: So critical capacity survives even if many spot instances are reclaimed at once.

strategy-price-capacity-optimized-select.core: Choosing the cheapest spot pool picks the pools most likely to be reclaimed. Price-capacity-optimised allocation weighs price against available capacity, picking pools that are both cheap and deep, so interruptions are far less likely.

first_principles.problem: Lowest-price strategies concentrate on shallow pools, which leads to frequent interruptions and churn.
truths: Cheap pools attract demand and get exhausted.
derivation: Accept a slightly higher price for **much lower churn**.

analogy.title: Choosing a checkout lane
analogy.story: The 'cheapest' lane with one slow cashier isn't best; a slightly pricier one with many open tills gets you through reliably.
analogy.breaks: Very narrow instance requirements limit diversification.

example.title: A Karpenter NodePool requirement

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Dozens of pools to choose from, so interruptions are rare.

example.outcome: spot that behaves almost like stable capacity.

check.q: Why is the lowest-price spot strategy risky?
check.a: The cheapest pools are often shallow and heavily demanded, so they're reclaimed more often.

the-split-architecture-weighted-nodepool.core: Express the on-demand/spot split through Kubernetes constraints: separate Karpenter NodePools (spot weighted higher for preference, on-demand as fallback) plus topology spread constraints on capacity type, so pods are distributed across both.

first_principles.problem: You can't tell Kubernetes directly to 'run 20% on on-demand'. You have to shape placement.
truths: Karpenter provisions nodes from NodePools by weight and requirements.
Topology spread distributes pods across labels.
derivation: A **spot NodePool** (higher weight) and an **on-demand NodePool** (fallback).

analogy.title: Seating guests across two halls
analogy.story: A rule says guests must be spread across both halls, so losing one hall never empties the party.
analogy.breaks: Spread constraints give approximate ratios, not exact percentages.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Replicas spread over spot and on-demand, which limits the blast radius.

code.text:
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 2
    topologyKey: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
    labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }

check.q: How do you spread pods across spot and on-demand nodes in Kubernetes?
check.a: With a topology spread constraint on the capacity-type node label.

handling-the-2-minute-warning.core: AWS sends an interruption notice two minutes before reclaiming a spot instance (plus earlier rebalance recommendations). Karpenter or the Node Termination Handler cordons and drains the node, pods shut down gracefully, and replacements start elsewhere.

first_principles.problem: Without handling, pods die abruptly, in-flight requests fail and state is lost.
truths: The notice arrives via instance metadata and EventBridge.
Draining respects PDBs and grace periods.
Replacement capacity takes time to start.
derivation: Enable **interruption handling** (Karpenter SQS queue or NTH).

analogy.title: A fire drill with a two-minute alarm
analogy.story: When the alarm sounds, everyone saves their work and walks out calmly to the other building.
analogy.breaks: Long-running requests or jobs over two minutes need checkpointing or retries.

example.title: An interruption sequence
flow: T-0: instance reclaimed, pods already moved

check.q: What should an application do on SIGTERM during a spot drain?
check.a: Stop accepting new work, finish or hand off in-flight requests, and exit within the grace period.
